title: AMD Crosses $1 Trillion as Meta's Muse AI Agent Ignites Chip Rally
excerpt: Intel jumped 12% and Arm surged 17% on Monday as the runaway success of Meta's Muse assistant convinced investors that AI agents will drive a surge in demand for central processing units.
body:
• AMD closed Monday at $615.52, up 9.9%, pushing its market capitalization above $1 trillion — the 14th U.S. company to reach the milestone and its first record close since June 30.
  • Intel jumped 12% and Arm soared 17% as investors bet that Meta's Muse AI agent will drive a surge in demand for central processing units used in AI inference.
  • Muse, launched Sept. 8, became the most-downloaded free iPhone app in the U.S., according to Sensor Tower, lifting Meta shares 11% in their biggest one-day gain in more than a year.

Advanced Micro Devices crossed $1 trillion in market value on Monday as a broad semiconductor rally — set off by Meta's runaway Muse AI agent — pushed Intel and Arm to double-digit gains and the Nasdaq to a record close.

AMD finished at $615.52, up 9.9% — its first record close since June 30, per Dow Jones Market Data — and has nearly quadrupled from a $255 billion valuation a year ago. Intel advanced 12% and Arm's U.S.-listed shares surged 17%, while the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbed about 3%.

Context & Background

Muse, Meta's personal AI assistant, launched Sept. 8 across iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp. Within ten days it overtook OpenAI's ChatGPT atop the U.S. App Store's free chart, with roughly 730,000 downloads in that window, per Sensor Tower data cited by Bloomberg. By this week it had passed 2.5 million downloads across iOS and Android combined, CNBC reported. Meta shares have risen 27% in September, on pace for their best month since January 2019.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=l_aT3g5Bceo

AI agents had an earlier viral moment this year with the open-source OpenClaw assistant, but it was hard for non-technical users to set up; Muse is far more accessible, and Meta has far more engineers developing it.

The stock-market logic is physical. Agents like Muse do not answer one question and stop; they run constantly in the background, executing sequential multi-step tasks — checking email, cross-referencing calendars, booking reservations — that demand continuous inference. That workload leans more on general-purpose CPUs than on the parallel processing where graphics chips dominate. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said last week the company can meet only about 50% of customer demand.

Arm has estimated the server CPU market can grow at more than 35% annually to reach $120 billion by 2030. AMD is more optimistic, projecting server CPUs could grow 50% through 2030, creating a $220 billion revenue opportunity.

"People are realizing Muse isn't a chatbot, and therefore the market is starting to understand that agentic workloads are different from those for AI-driven searches and conversations."

— Daniel O'Regan, analyst, Mizuho

Impact & Analysis

Mizuho's Daniel O'Regan said AI agents had driven a "full-blown feeding frenzy" in chip and networking stocks on Monday, reflecting that investors were "finally starting to connect the dots on what" the Muse launch signals for AI infrastructure demand. He added that Muse's success has investors asking when OpenAI, Anthropic and Google will launch similar agents — "that's when the infrastructure math starts to get crazy."

Wall Street had treated AI infrastructure as a graphics-chip story, with Nvidia at the center. The world's most valuable public company is worth more than $5 trillion. Monday suggested the trade is widening: AMD joins Nvidia, Broadcom and Micron among U.S. chipmakers valued at $1 trillion or more.

The rally capped a sharp sentiment reversal: one week earlier, warnings from OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about advanced AI risks helped trigger a global tech selloff. On Monday, Meta added $192 billion in market value, the Magnificent Seven ETF hit its first record since May, the Nasdaq rose 2.3% to a record, the S&P 500 gained 1.5% and the Dow added 366 points. Tech stocks also got a lift after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he and China's vice premier He Lifeng had agreed to an AI dialogue.

"Muse is Meta's most consequential consumer product in years — the clearest attempt yet to build a non-advertising revenue stream."

— Youssef Squali, analyst, Truist

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

The CPU rally lands close to home for the Indian diaspora. Indian-origin engineers make up a large share of the semiconductor workforce at AMD, Intel and Arm, both in Silicon Valley and in India's chip-design hubs, and U.S.-listed equities have become a growing allocation for Indian retail investors through cross-border investing apps.

What's Next

The immediate question is whether AMD can hold above the $1 trillion line and whether Muse's download surge converts into sustained usage. The bigger test comes with the next wave of launches: if OpenAI, Anthropic or Google ship their own consumer agents, CPU demand estimates get a second leg. Chipmakers' next earnings reports will show whether order books are catching up with the market's enthusiasm.
